## [1]{.chapter-step} The question {#sec-question}

How do you measure the effect of a treatment when there is nothing to compare
against — you cannot both give someone a drug and withhold it?

## [2]{.chapter-step} Intuition {#sec-intuition}

Hospitals are full of sick people. Does that mean hospitals damage your health?

The question sounds silly, but its structure is exactly that of most business
questions. Users who installed the app spend more — does the app increase
revenue? Employees who took the training perform better — is that the
training, or is it that strong performers get sent to training?

The problem is the same every time: **the groups differed before any treatment
happened**. Comparing their outcomes adds the treatment effect to that
pre-existing gap, and nothing in the comparison separates the two.

This forces a shift in how the question is posed. The right question is not
"how do the treated differ from the untreated". The right question is "what
would have happened to **these same** people had they not been treated".

The second question is about data we do not have. That is why causal inference
is a discipline about recovering missing data, rather than about describing
the data in hand.

## [3]{.chapter-step} Formalism {#sec-formalism}

### Potential outcomes

Every unit $i$ has **two** outcomes defined:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_i(0) &\quad \text{what would happen without treatment} \\
Y_i(1) &\quad \text{what would happen with it}
\end{aligned}
$$

The causal effect for that unit is $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$.

We observe only one of the two, depending on the realized assignment
$T_i \in \{0, 1\}$:

$$
Y_i = T_i \cdot Y_i(1) + (1 - T_i) \cdot Y_i(0).
$$

::: {.recall}
The observed outcome is a **collapse** of the potential-outcome pair. The other
half — the {{< term counterfactual >}} — is not merely unknown, it is
unobservable in principle. This is the [fundamental problem of causal
inference](/glossary.qmd#term-fundamental-problem).
:::

### What can actually be estimated

The individual effect $\tau_i$ is never available. Averages are:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{ATE} &= E[Y(1) - Y(0)] \\
\text{ATT} &= E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid T = 1] \\
\text{CATE}(x) &= E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X = x]
\end{aligned}
$$

{{< term ate >}} answers "what happens if we treat everyone".
{{< term att >}} answers "what did treatment do for those who got it". Under a
heterogeneous effect these are different numbers, and substituting one for the
other is not a rounding error.

### Where the bias comes from

The naive difference in means decomposes into two parts. This identity is the
center of the chapter:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{E[Y \mid T=1] - E[Y \mid T=0]}_{\text{what we computed}}
&= \underbrace{E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid T=1]}_{\text{ATT — what we wanted}} \\[0.6em]
&\quad + \underbrace{E[Y(0) \mid T=1] - E[Y(0) \mid T=0]}_{\text{selection bias}}
\end{aligned}
$$

The second term is how much the groups would have differed **with no treatment
at all**. It is unobservable, because it is made of counterfactuals.

::: {.recall}
Naive difference = ATT + {{< term selection-bias >}}. Selection bias is not
noise and not sampling error: it does not shrink as the sample grows. More
data makes a wrong answer more precise, not more correct.
:::

### What has to be assumed

::: {.assumption name="Ignorability"}
$$(Y(0), Y(1)) \perp T \mid X$$

Within each level of the covariates $X$, treatment is as good as randomly
assigned. In a {{< term rct >}} this holds by construction, because a coin does
the assigning. In observational data it is an untestable assumption: the data
can neither confirm nor refute it, only subject-matter knowledge can argue for
it.
:::

::: {.assumption name="Positivity"}
$$0 < P(T = 1 \mid X = x) < 1 \quad \text{for all } x$$

Every unit has a nonzero chance of landing in either group. If at some $x$
everyone is treated or nobody is, there is no counterfactual available there —
and no method repairs that.
:::

::: {.assumption name="SUTVA"}
A unit's outcome does not depend on what was assigned to other units, and the
treatment exists in a single version. Violated by network effects and by
marketplaces, where units compete for a shared resource.
:::

## [4]{.chapter-step} Verify with code {#sec-verification}

Let us check the identity from step 3 on a simulation where the truth is known
by construction. Two datasets with the **same** true effect $\tau = 2$: in the
first, assignment is random; in the second, a confounder drives it.

```{python}
#| label: simulate

TRUE_ATE = 2.0

rct = randomized_trial(n=4000, ate=TRUE_ATE, seed=7)
obs = confounded(n=4000, ate=TRUE_ATE, confounding=3.0, seed=7)

pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "design": ["Randomized", "Confounded"],
        "true ATE": [true_ate(rct), true_ate(obs)],
        "true ATT": [true_att(rct), true_att(obs)],
        "naive difference": [naive_diff(rct), naive_diff(obs)],
        "bias": [naive_diff(rct) - true_ate(rct), naive_diff(obs) - true_ate(obs)],
    }
).round(3)
```

The true effect is 2 in both designs. The naive difference recovers it in the
first and lands near 6 in the second — three times the truth, with the bias
term alone twice the size of the real effect. The difference is not in the data
and not in the sample size; it is entirely in the **assignment mechanism**.

Let us see where the bias came from. The confounder $x$ pushes both the
probability of treatment and the outcome itself, so the groups separate along
$x$ before treatment has done anything at all.

```{python}
#| label: fig-confounding
#| fig-cap: "The confounder pulls the groups apart along x. The vertical gap between the clouds is the effect and the bias added together, and no amount of looking separates them."

obs_plot = obs.assign(group=np.where(obs["t"] == 1, "Treated", "Control"))

fig = px.scatter(
    obs_plot,
    x="x",
    y="y",
    color="group",
    opacity=0.45,
    # Plotly switches to WebGL above ~1000 points on its own. SVG keeps the
    # chart working without a GPU and keeps it recolorable on theme toggle.
    render_mode="svg",
    color_discrete_map={"Control": C.control, "Treated": C.treated},
    labels={"x": "Confounder x", "y": "Observed outcome y"},
)
fig.update_traces(marker=dict(size=5, line=dict(width=0)))
apply_theme(fig)
fig.update_layout(height=420)
fig
```

Now the same thing in terms of the identity. Split the naive difference into
ATT and selection bias — in a simulation both parts are computable, because
the potential outcomes are known.

```{python}
#| label: fig-decomposition
#| fig-cap: "Decomposition of the naive difference. Under randomization the selection-bias segment is zero by construction, so the naive estimate lands on the truth."

parts = {"Randomized": decompose(rct), "Confounded": decompose(obs)}
designs = list(parts)

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_bar(
    name="ATT — the causal effect",
    x=designs,
    y=[parts[d]["att"] for d in designs],
    marker_color=C.treated,
)
fig.add_bar(
    name="Selection bias",
    x=designs,
    y=[parts[d]["bias"] for d in designs],
    marker_color=C.bias,
)
fig.update_layout(
    barmode="relative",
    height=400,
    yaxis_title="Contribution to the naive difference",
)
truth_line(fig, y=TRUE_ATE, label="True ATE = 2")
apply_theme(fig)
fig
```

The segments add up to exactly the naive difference. In the randomized design
the second segment is degenerate — the coin knows nothing about the potential
outcomes, so $E[Y(0) \mid T=1] = E[Y(0) \mid T=0]$.

::: {.quiz question="The sample grows from 4,000 to 400,000 observations. What happens to the bias in the second design?"}
Nothing. Selection bias is a property of the **assignment mechanism**, not of
the sample size. Only precision improves: the confidence interval tightens
around the very same wrong number.

This is what separates bias from random error, and it is why "we have millions
of rows" is not an argument in a causal question.
:::

## [5]{.chapter-step} Explorable {#sec-explorable}

The table above shows two points: confounding present, confounding absent. The
interesting part is the whole transition between them.

→ [**Bias from confounding**](/explorables/confounding-bias.qmd) — move a
slider to vary the confounder's strength from zero and watch the truth and the
naive estimate separate. At zero the design degenerates into a randomized
experiment.

## [6]{.chapter-step} When it breaks {#sec-failure}

| What happens | Why it hurts | Signal in the data |
|---|---|---|
| The driver of selection is unobserved | Controlling for covariates cannot help — there is nothing to control | None. The data looks fine |
| Positivity is violated | At some $x$ there is no counterfactual at all | Propensity estimates pile up near 0 or 1 |
| SUTVA is violated | The control group is contaminated by the treatment | Network structure, shared resource, marketplace |
| Effect is heterogeneous but ATE is reported | The number is right, the decision is wrong | ATT diverges noticeably from ATE |
| Controlling for a collider | Adding a control **creates** bias | The estimate moves when a "sensible" variable is added |

The last row is the treacherous one. The instinct that "more controls cannot
hurt" is wrong: controlling for a variable that is a consequence of both
treatment and outcome opens a path that did not exist. Covered in the chapter
on DAGs.

::: {.quiz question="Why not simply put every available variable into the regression?"}
Because variables come in kinds that must be handled differently.
Controlling for a {{< term confounder >}} removes bias; controlling for a
collider creates it. The data cannot tell them apart — only an assumed causal
structure can.

The consequence: choosing controls is a decision made **before** looking at
the data, on the basis of subject-matter knowledge.
:::

## [7]{.chapter-step} In my own words {#sec-summary}

Causal inference starts by admitting the necessary data does not exist and
never will. Every unit has two potential outcomes, exactly one is observed, so
the individual effect is unavailable in principle.

Averages rescue us — but only if we know how treatment was assigned. A naive
difference in means always equals the real effect plus selection bias.
Randomization zeroes the second term by construction, and that single property
is its entire value.

Everything else in the course is a way to zero out selection bias where
randomization is impossible. Each method buys that with an assumption the data
cannot check.

::: {.recall}
Methods of causal inference differ less in their mathematics than in **which
untestable assumption** they demand in exchange for randomization. Judge a
method by how plausible its assumption is in the problem at hand, not by how
sophisticated its machinery looks.
:::
